claims.text: A nanoscale coherent L12-ordered Fe-Ti precipitate phase can be formed within an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn high-entropy alloy matrix.
The L12 Fe-Ti precipitates will increase coercivity above 100 Oe.
Coherent precipitates will pin domain walls through magneto-elastic strain fields.
The fcc matrix and L12 Fe-Ti precipitates will form a hard-magnetic/soft-magnetic exchange-spring interface.
The initial single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn alloy has a suppressed orbital moment and low magnetic anisotropy.
The initial alloy has coercivity significantly below 100 Oe.
The initial alloy exhibits ferromagnetic ordering well above room temperature.
Aging between 600 and 800 degrees Celsius can nucleate and grow 5–20 nm coherent L12 Fe-Ti precipitates.
The proposed aging treatment can preserve continuity of the fcc matrix without bulk phase separation.
High vacuum or inert argon will prevent oxidation during aging.
Controlled furnace cooling will preserve precipitate coherency.
The L12 Fe-Ti phase has higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy than the fcc matrix.
Local variations in magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magneto-elastic coupling make the precipitates strong domain-wall pinning centers.
The exchange-spring interface will create a domain-wall depinning energy greater than thermal energy at room temperature.
The precipitates can raise coercivity without significantly reducing saturation magnetization or Curie temperature.
The aged alloy will have a squareness ratio greater than 0.3 and a Curie temperature above 400 K.
A kink in the hysteresis loop will indicate exchange coupling between the two phases.
The unaged single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Ti alloy has coercivity below 20 Oe because it has low anisotropy and lacks pinning sites.
Precipitates larger than 50 nm or incoherent precipitates will have lower pinning efficiency and may reduce coercivity.
Excess Ti can destabilize the fcc matrix and produce a brittle BCC phase.

contradictions.description: The initial matrix is specified as Fe-Co-Ni-Mn without Ti, yet the precipitate is Fe-Ti and the intervention only applies thermal aging rather than adding Ti. The baseline instead identifies the unaged alloy as Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Ti, leaving the starting composition internally inconsistent.

The boundary permits coherent or semi-coherent precipitates, whereas the falsification rule treats incoherency as falsification even though it would mean the required intervention state was not achieved rather than directly disproving the proposed mechanism.
